extracted.intended_audience: advanced philosophy students and scholars studying Kantian teleology and the Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and evaluation of Kant's arguments about purposiveness, teleology, and the limits of theoretical and practical Reason in the Critique of Judgment. Focuses on the distinction between determinant and reflective judgement and on how purposiveness is to be treated epistemically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant vs. reflective Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Dogmatic (determinant) procedure treats a concept as contained under another concept of the Object and constitutive for judgement; critical (reflective) procedure considers a concept only in reference to our cognitive faculties and subjective conditions of thinking it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinant judgements require assurance of objective reality before subsuming objects under a concept; reflective judgements examine how our faculties make the concept necessary for cognition without claiming objective authority. This distinction governs whether teleological concepts can be treated as constitutive principles (for determining objects) or only as regulative/maxims for reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of a natural purpose not susceptible of proof (not constitutive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of a thing as a natural purpose embraces both natural necessity and contingency and therefore cannot be dogmatically proven to have objective reality; it is problematical (conceptus ratiocinans) unless confirmed by Reason (conceptus ratiocinatus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the concept mixes necessity and contingency it is transcendent for determinant judgement; synthetical predicates about whether natural purposes are designed or undesigned remain problematical. Any attempt to treat this concept as constitutive for objective claims about nature fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept of purposiveness as a critical/regulative principle for reflective Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: While not constitutive for determinant judgement, the concept of purposiveness is a critical principle of Reason and a necessary regulative maxim for the reflective judgement when investigating organised products of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim is indispensable for empirical investigation of organised beings: it guides research by representing natural products as if produced according to design, thereby suggesting lines of inquiry and revealing laws otherwise hidden. Its validity is subjective (attached to human cognition) rather than objective proof of teleological causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology yields only subjective warrant for thinking a designing cause (not objective proof of God)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological investigation can show that, given the constitution of our cognitive faculties, we cannot think the possibility of many natural products except by representing them as products of a designing cause; this is a subjective maxim for judgement, not an objective proof that an intelligent original Being exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes the permissible subjective claim—'we cannot otherwise make comprehensible the purposiveness of many natural things than by thinking an intelligent cause'—from the dogmatic objective assertion 'There is a God.' Teleology thus leads to theology only as a regulative, not constitutive, result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of treating the Technic of nature dogmatically (mechanism insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot dogmatically derive purposive unity in nature from mere mechanism; to posit a mechanistic ground for purposiveness would require proving the impossibility of unity of purpose resulting from mechanism, which cannot be done within our cognitive limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before appealing beyond nature to a designing cause one must show mechanism cannot yield purposiveness; Kant argues we cannot complete that proof. Therefore mechanistic explanations (without design) are insufficient as dogmatic solutions to purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epicurean and Spinozist explanations fail to establish purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Epicurus (blind chance) denies intentionality and thus explains away purposiveness as mere mechanism; Spinoza reduces purposiveness to accidents inhering in a single substrate and thereby removes contingency and intelligence required for a unity of purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epicureanism leaves the 'illusion' of teleological judgement unexplained; Spinozism preserves ontological unity but not the specific unity of purpose that implies an intelligent cause. Both are given as anti-patterns for a satisfactory teleological account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hylozoism is circular and cannot be established a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Deriving purposiveness from the 'life of matter' (hylozoism) is circular because the possibility of living matter cannot be thought a priori; we only know life through organised beings, so explaining purposiveness by life of matter presupposes what must be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hylozoism thus fails to provide an a priori ground for purposiveness: it yields a circular explanation and cannot establish objective reality for teleological concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Understanding's peculiarity: discursive understanding forces purposive representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Our understanding is discursive (proceeds from universal to particular) and cannot determine the particular; therefore, because particulars must nonetheless accord with universals, we represent their accordance as contingent and hence as purposive—we must think of certain natural products 'as if' designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant contrasts discursive (human) understanding with a possible intuitive understanding that would proceed from whole to parts; the human method makes purposiveness a necessary regulative idea for judgment of organised nature. This identifies a cognitive source for teleological thinking rather than an ontological claim about nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between possibility and actuality is subjective and gives rise to regulative Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: For human cognition, the distinction between possible and actual rests on our faculties (concepts versus sensible intuition); ideas like the absolutely necessary Being are indispensable regulative Ideas of Reason but remain problematical and not constitutive of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subjective distinction explains why Reason posits unconditioned principles (e.g., necessary Being, freedom) as regulative: they guide cognition and moral thought but do not constitute objective knowledge about things in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness combines necessity and contingency, making it transcendent for determinant judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of purposiveness (as of a natural product) simultaneously involves natural necessity (laws) and contingency (form relative to those laws), so if judged determinately it would require grounds both for the thing's possibility and for the possibility of nature itself—grounds not obtainable from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this dual character, purposiveness cannot be given objective reality within determinant judgement; attempts to do so make the concept transcendent and lead to insoluble questions about origins and grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the whole as cause of the parts (definition of purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the representation of a whole contains the ground of the possibility of the connexion of its parts, the representation of the whole is treated as the cause of the parts; a product whose cause is determined by the representation of the effect is called a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion explains how purposiveness is conceived: purposiveness arises when the form of a whole (representation) is used as a principle for the possibility of its parts. It underpins the teleological way we judge organised beings, by treating the end (whole) as a kind of determining ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxim of judgement as a heuristic for discovering natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting the maxim of thinking nature's organised products as if produced by design is a useful guiding thread for empirical inquiry: it may reveal laws and regularities that would remain hidden given the limits of our insight into mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant allows the reflective maxim to be extended experimentally to 'nature as a whole' as a heuristic, though he emphasizes this is not indispensable and does not license objective assertions about supernatural causes. Its value is methodological rather than ontological.
